GOSHIST111.name: Modern History
GOSHIST111.substantiveEvidence: Surveys economic, political and cultural developments from 1815 to the present while questioning the meaning and periodization of modernity. Students examine industrialization, political ideologies, nationalism, imperialism, migration, world wars, revolution, decolonization, the Cold War and globalization. Historical research and essays connect specific questions to evidence. A group project analyzes historical visions of the future as products of their own contexts and compares them with subsequent developments.
GOSHIST111.topics: Modernity and periodization; Industrialization and reform; Political ideologies and nationalism; Migration and imperialism; National, class, gender and racial identities; World wars; Russian Revolution and Soviet history; Democracy and dictatorship; Cold War; Decolonization; Globalization; Historical visions of the future
GOSHIST111.methods: Historical contextualization; Primary- and secondary-source analysis; Source triangulation; Historical research-question development

GOSHIST112.name: Histories of Gender
GOSHIST112.substantiveEvidence: Studies gendered histories and lives in North America from the nineteenth century to the present, centering storytelling and intersectionality. Queer and heteronormative narratives connect slavery, family, sexuality, health, incarceration and contemporary backlash to resistance and activism. Students interpret primary sources and scholarship, interview older queer people, contribute to the Walking with Pride activist artwork, and conduct an original research project in a chosen format.
GOSHIST112.topics: Gender and intersectionality; Body sovereignty; Heteronormativity and compulsory heterosexuality; Homonationalism; Rainbow capitalism; Masculinity and sexuality; Queer ageing and memory; Slavery and racialized gender histories; Family and socialization; Health and pathologization; Media bias and book bans; Incarceration; Queer activism and resistance
GOSHIST112.methods: Historical primary-source research; Intersectional analysis; Oral-history interviewing; Critical interpretation of memoir and cultural representations; Arts-based research; Community-engaged activist art; Reflective analysis

GOSHIST211.name: History of Empires
GOSHIST211.substantiveEvidence: Examines empires comparatively across global history, from ancient Persia, Rome and China to early-modern and modern imperial powers and contemporary claims to imperial status. Students analyze expansion, administration, military and economic systems, legitimacy, ideology, culture, decline and legacies. The course combines theories of empire with historically specific cases, historiographical discussion, source analysis and an independently developed research essay.
GOSHIST211.topics: Concepts and theories of empire; Imperial rise, expansion and decline; Administration and succession; Military and economic structures; Imperial ideologies and legitimacy; Culture and empire; Ancient and medieval empires; European overseas empires; Modern Asian and Eurasian empires; American power; Contemporary and future empires; Imperial legacies
GOSHIST211.methods: Comparative historical analysis; Historiographical analysis; Primary- and secondary-source analysis; Historical research-question development

GOSHIST213.name: Ways of War
GOSHIST213.substantiveEvidence: Surveys Western warfare from antiquity to the present and examines the contested claim that a distinctive military trajectory helped produce Western global dominance. Weapons, technology, strategy, tactics, institutions and soldiers' experience are studied across land, sea and air warfare. Research analyzes a strategic text, a commander's performance or a battle from the individual soldier's perspective, using primary sources and historical scholarship.
GOSHIST213.topics: Western warfare and global power; Ancient infantry and Roman warfare; Medieval warfare; Gunpowder and naval warfare; Overseas conquest; Dynastic and national warfare; Industrialization of war; World wars; Cold War and nuclear strategy; Guerrilla warfare and terrorism; Military leadership; Soldiers' experience, morale and cohesion; Future warfare
GOSHIST213.methods: Primary- and secondary-source analysis; Historiographical critique of strategic texts; Historical analysis of military command; Soldier-centered battle analysis; Analysis of diaries, memoirs and combat accounts

GOSHIST311.name: Native American Histories
GOSHIST311.substantiveEvidence: Studies Native American social and cultural histories from the nineteenth century to the present through Indigenous perspectives and collaborative inquiry. Boarding schools, institutional violence, family separation and intergenerational trauma are connected to contemporary resistance, resurgence, food sovereignty and cultural expression. Storytelling, relational accountability and reciprocity inform work with Indigenous peers and knowledge holders. Arts-based collaborations and a public-history project develop respectful, accessible accounts of historical and contemporary issues.
GOSHIST311.topics: Indigenous histories and ways of knowing; Colonialism and white saviourism; Indian wars; Boarding schools and childhood trauma; Institutional confinement; Adoption and blood quantum; Gendered violence and missing Indigenous people; Traditional ecological knowledge; Food sovereignty; Decolonization and Indigenization; Cultural resistance and resurgence; Indigenous storytelling and public history
GOSHIST311.methods: Indigenous storywork and relational historical inquiry; Primary-source and oral-history analysis; Arts-based collaborative inquiry; Photo/Voice photography and audio narratives; Historical contextualization of contemporary issues; Public-history multimedia production

GOSHIST312.name: Researching the “American Century”
GOSHIST312.substantiveEvidence: Guides students through the full arc of historical inquiry, from formulating research questions to engaging critically with sources. Emphasises methodological rigour and interdisciplinary thinking and culminates in a substantial research paper.

GOSSOCI111.name: Introduction to Sociology
GOSSOCI111.substantiveEvidence: Introduces sociological reasoning through classical theories, their historical settings and perspectives that address exclusions from the discipline. Students connect solidarity, modernity, identity, social boundaries, networks and stratification to race, gender, migration and inequality in education and work. An individual analysis applies a course concept to contemporary social life without original data collection. A group paper develops a sociological question and analyzes a social problem using theory and academic literature.
GOSSOCI111.topics: Sociological imagination and knowledge; Social structure and socialization; Classical social theory; Colonialism and the formation of sociology; Solidarity and modernity; Identity, belonging and othering; Groups and social networks; Capital, class and mobility; Race and gender inequality; Global inequality and migration; Education and labour-market inequality
GOSSOCI111.methods: Theory-guided sociological case analysis; Comparative analysis of sociological perspectives; Library-based social-science research; Sociological research-question formulation

GOSSOCI212.name: Qualitative Research Methodology
GOSSOCI212.substantiveEvidence: Develops qualitative inquiry from research design and preparation through data collection, management, analysis and dissemination. Students examine methodological foundations, ethics, positionality and reflexivity alongside interviews, focus groups, ethnography, documentary and visual approaches. Coding, thematic interpretation and NVivo support analysis. Research teams formulate a question, collect and analyze qualitative evidence, and report their methodological decisions, findings and limitations in staged assignments.
GOSSOCI212.topics: Qualitative knowledge and research design; Ethics, positionality and reflexivity; Mixed methods; Participatory research; Interview and focus-group approaches; Ethnography and participant observation; Documentary and archival sources; Visual and participatory media; Coding and thematic interpretation; Qualitative research dissemination
GOSSOCI212.methods: Qualitative research design; Interviews; Focus groups; Ethnography and participant observation; Documentary and archival analysis; Visual-data analysis; Participatory video and drawing; Transcription; Qualitative coding; Thematic analysis; NVivo-supported analysis; Reflexive methodological evaluation

GOSSOCI214.name: Modern Sociology
GOSSOCI214.substantiveEvidence: Examines twentieth-century and contemporary social theory alongside critical accounts of modernity, colonialism and disciplinary exclusion. Functionalism, critical theory, Black feminist thought, phenomenology, symbolic interactionism and Bourdieu's work are read with postcolonial, decolonial and Indigenous perspectives. Students compare theories and apply them to empirical cases, including visual material. An individual research paper develops a theoretically grounded interpretation of a selected social phenomenon.
GOSSOCI214.topics: Modernity and Eurocentrism; Functionalism; Frankfurt School critical theory; Black feminist thought and intersectionality; Social construction of reality; Symbolic interactionism; Stigma and othering; Social space, capital and art; Coloniality and postcolonialism; Decolonial and Indigenous sociology; Gender and power
GOSSOCI214.methods: Close reading of social theory; Comparative theoretical analysis; Theory-guided empirical case analysis; Visual sociological analysis; Literature-based sociological research

GOSSOCI215.name: Social Movements & Environmental Justice
GOSSOCI215.substantiveEvidence: Focuses on social movement theories and environmental justice. Uses case studies from the Environmental Justice Atlas and integrates perspectives such as feminism, anti‑colonialism, degrowth and environmental peacebuilding to encourage civic engagement.

GOSSOCI311.name: New Issues in Contemporary Social Theory
GOSSOCI311.substantiveEvidence: Focuses on civil society through critical, neo-functionalist and decolonial social theory. Students examine social trust, capital, hegemony, public spheres, solidarity, social movements and civil repair across political and regional contexts. An experience report relates personal engagement or observation to course concepts. An individual research project uses theoretical and empirical sources to analyze a civil-society organization, movement, initiative or related phenomenon.
GOSSOCI311.topics: Civil society; Social trust and social capital; Hegemony; Critical theory; Public spheres, digital publics and counterpublics; Solidarity and civil repair; Civil sphere; Social movements and intersectionality; Migrant solidarity; Civil society under authoritarianism; Decolonial critique; Public sociology
GOSSOCI311.methods: Comparative social-theory analysis; Theory-guided empirical case analysis; Document and secondary-source analysis; Structured reflection on civil-society engagement or observation; Sociological research design

MCCCOMM111.name: The Art of Rhetorical Communication
MCCCOMM111.substantiveEvidence: Teaches rhetorical analysis and persuasive communication through classical history, theory and practice. Students study Greek and Roman rhetoric, the five canons, types of discourse, persuasive appeals, argumentation and fallacies. Written exercises, debates and public speeches develop invention, arrangement, style, memory and delivery. An applied project creates narrative and storytelling material for an immersive educational setting concerned with Zeeland's climate and community.
MCCCOMM111.topics: Greek and Roman rhetoric; Deliberative, forensic and epideictic discourse; Logos, ethos and pathos; Invention, arrangement, style, memory and delivery; Argumentation and fallacies; Tropes and schemes; Stasis and enthymemes; Persuasive speech; Narrative and storytelling; Immersive educational communication
MCCCOMM111.methods: Rhetorical text analysis; Stasis analysis; Argument invention and arrangement; Stylistic analysis and composition; Structured debate; Persuasive speechwriting and delivery; Educational storytelling design

MCCCOMM112.name: Dutch
MCCCOMM112.substantiveEvidence: Develops beginner Dutch for everyday oral and written communication while introducing Dutch culture. Speaking and listening receive particular emphasis, supported by pronunciation, vocabulary, grammar, reading and functional writing. Students practise introductions, family conversations, shopping, travel and leisure through dialogues, role-play and short written tasks. Cultural work includes research and presentations in English, engagement with Dutch film and music, and comparison with students’ own cultural contexts.
MCCCOMM112.topics: Dutch pronunciation and spelling; Everyday vocabulary for introductions, family, shopping, travel and leisure; Verb conjugation and the perfect tense; Pronouns and possession; Negation; Main- and subordinate-clause word order; Adjectives, comparatives and superlatives; Functional reading and writing; Everyday Dutch cultural practices; Cross-cultural comparison
MCCCOMM112.methods: Dutch pronunciation practice; Dialogue construction and conversational role-play; Functional writing in Dutch; Comparative cultural analysis

MCCCOMM211.name: Style & Meaning
MCCCOMM211.substantiveEvidence: Studies how linguistic choices produce meaning and interpretive effects, principally in literary texts but also in nonfiction. Students connect linguistic description to interpretation across grammar, discourse and cognition. Stylistic frameworks address foregrounding, dialogue, narration, modality, transitivity, deixis, schemas, construal and text worlds. Frequent analysis exercises lead to an original, research-supported stylistic analysis of a selected text.
MCCCOMM211.topics: Foregrounding and deviation; Morphology, syntax and lexical semantics; Register and cohesion; Dialogue and turn-taking; Cooperative principle; Speech and thought presentation; Modality and point of view; Transitivity and ideology; Narrative urgency; Figure and ground; Deixis and deictic shift; Schemas, scripts and prototypes; Cognitive grammar and construal; Text-world theory; Negation and lacuna
MCCCOMM211.methods: Linguistic stylistic analysis; Close textual analysis; Discourse and conversation analysis; Speech and thought presentation analysis; Modality and transitivity analysis; Deictic and cognitive-grammar analysis; Text-world analysis; Framework-based interpretation supported by retrievable textual evidence

MCCCOMM212.name: Communicating the Climate Crisis
MCCCOMM212.substantiveEvidence: Examines how the climate crisis is communicated and contested. Analyzes texts, films, exhibitions, protest art, slogans and social media alongside theory and case studies, teaching students to dissect arguments and culminating in a project where students enter the debate.

MCCCOMM213.name: Rhetoric in Action
MCCCOMM213.substantiveEvidence: Applies rhetoric through community-engaged work with local primary-school children. Students develop their own public-speaking, debating and storytelling skills, then design and iteratively refine age-appropriate teaching activities with school partners. On-site coaching and a final public-speaking event connect rhetorical education to civic participation and confidence. Structured reflection examines reciprocity, cultural sensitivity, personal development and the practical challenges of community-engaged teaching.
MCCCOMM213.topics: Public work of rhetoric; Community-engaged learning and reciprocity; Public speaking and debate; Storytelling; Children's rhetorical confidence and civic participation; Rhetorical teaching and coaching; Cultural sensitivity; Collaboration with community partners; Experiential and reflective learning
MCCCOMM213.methods: Public-speaking and debate coaching; Storytelling exercises; Iterative design and revision of teaching materials; Practice-based rhetorical instruction; Gibbs reflective-cycle analysis; Public-speaking event design and evaluation

MCCCOMM311.name: Persuasive Communication
MCCCOMM311.substantiveEvidence: Examines contemporary persuasion through communication studies, social psychology and ethical analysis, then applies it in community-engaged work. Students study coactive persuasion, framing, argumentation, cognitive shortcuts and verbal and nonverbal communication. Projects with the Delta Climate Centre and Vlissingen municipality develop communication encouraging sustainable and circular lifestyles. An individual research paper evaluates selected persuasion tools through literature review, field research diaries and reflective analysis of their use.
MCCCOMM311.topics: Persuasion models and psychology; Ethics of persuasion; Coactive persuasion; Verbal and nonverbal communication; Message framing; Argumentation; Cognitive shortcuts and nudging; Science and sustainability communication; Circular lifestyles; Community-engaged communication
MCCCOMM311.methods: Persuasive-message design; Communication consulting and implementation; Literature review; Qualitative research diaries; Action research; Reflective case-study analysis; Gibbs reflective cycle

MCCCOMM312.name: Creative Communication Laboratory
MCCCOMM312.substantiveEvidence: Studies and develops creative communication through poetry, performance and critically articulated artistic practice. Students move from lyric foundations to constrained and experimental forms, attending to sound, rhythm, imagery, voice and embodiment. Close reading and creative workshops lead into an independent traditional or hybrid project grounded in scholarship and aesthetic traditions. Revision and reflection require students to justify formal, conceptual and procedural choices.
MCCCOMM312.topics: Meaning and formal experimentation; Lyric poetry; Poetic sound and rhythm; Imagery and voice; Embodiment and performance; Constraint and formal deviation; Experimental poetry; Hybrid and digitally mediated forms; Creative process and revision; Aesthetic traditions and conceptual coherence
MCCCOMM312.methods: Close poetic reading and listening; Constraint-based composition; Poetic and performative experimentation; Structured drafting and revision; Critical analysis of creative decisions; Independent practice-based creative inquiry

MCCHEAM111.name: Introduction to Western Art History
MCCHEAM111.substantiveEvidence: Surveys Western art from late-medieval and Renaissance painting to contemporary practice. Students relate artists, styles and movements to social, religious, political and cultural change, with sustained attention to the close examination of paintings. Practical assignments develop analysis of composition, space, form, tone and colour. A term paper studies a painting on location, combining visual interpretation with art-historical evidence and terminology.
MCCHEAM111.topics: Late-medieval and Renaissance art; Mannerism; Baroque and Rococo; Enlightenment and Romanticism; Realism and Impressionism; Post-Impressionism, Symbolism and Art Nouveau; Modernism and Cubism; Interwar art; Postwar and postmodern art; Contemporary art; Artistic form and historical context
MCCHEAM111.methods: Close visual analysis of paintings; Composition, space, form, tone and colour analysis; On-site artwork study; Historical contextualization; Art-historical text analysis

MCCHEAM112.name: Introduction to World Archaeology
MCCHEAM112.substantiveEvidence: Examines how making objects shaped communities and identities from the Neolithic through antiquity across Europe, Asia and Africa. Artefacts, production technologies and craft organization are interpreted in relation to social status, religion, gender, exchange and environmental settings. Students produce an archaeological catalogue description and technical drawings, research a craft-related question and design a hands-on educational game. A small contemporary-archaeology project collects local material evidence and proposes a testable interpretation.
MCCHEAM112.topics: Materiality, craft and cognition; Settlement and landscape; Neolithic and Bronze Age communities; Craft production and social hierarchy; Trade and exchange; Pottery and iconography; Seals, textiles and elite identities; Domestic and urban craft spaces; Archaeological interpretation; Ancient technology and community identity; Contemporary archaeology
MCCHEAM112.methods: Artefact observation, measurement and cataloguing; Archaeological technical drawing; Visual and stylistic analysis; Comparative material-culture analysis; Archaeological database and literature research; Material-evidence-based argumentation; Archaeological educational-game design; Contemporary archaeological data collection and hypothesis development

MCCHEAM211.name: African Art & Heritage
MCCHEAM211.substantiveEvidence: Introduces African art and heritage with particular attention to western African visual traditions and their cultural, religious and social meanings. Students study sculpture, masks and other forms across regional contexts before tracing African art's role in European modernism, the Harlem Renaissance and African artistic renewal. Colonial dispossession, museum collecting and restitution form a major later strand. An independent paper develops a research question supported by scholarly evidence.
MCCHEAM211.topics: Western African artistic traditions; Sculpture, masks and visual languages; Art, religion and social authority; Regional traditions in Nigeria, the Niger region, Atlantic forests and Congo; African influences on European modernism; Harlem Renaissance and diaspora; Art Nègre and the Ecole de Dakar; Colonial looting; Universal museums; Museum acquisition and display; Restitution and repatriation
MCCHEAM211.methods: Visual and contextual art-historical analysis; Comparative interpretation of artistic traditions; Analysis of primary artistic and critical texts; Heritage-restitution case analysis; Scholarly literature review and annotated bibliography; Independent art-historical research

MCCHEAM212.name: Renaissance Italy & Global Mediterranean
MCCHEAM212.substantiveEvidence: This course examines the painting, sculpture, and architecture of Renaissance Italy and the extensive artistic connections that linked the Italian peninsula to other regions of the world. By exploring a range of geographical contexts, from the Islamic courts of the Eastern Mediterranean and the commercial routes connecting Europe, Asia, and Africa to the newly encountered territories of the Americas, students will examine how trade, colonization, and cross-cultural exchange shaped the production and meaning of Renaissance art.

MCCHEAM213.name: Greek Archaeology
MCCHEAM213.substantiveEvidence: The invention of democracy in classical Greece changed the nature of community decision-making, perhaps forever. This process is reflected in the material culture of the period. By examining the archaeology of community & democracy in early-democratic Greece, this course goes in search of ancient lessons for the modern world.

MCCHEAM312.name: Modern Art & Modern Museums
MCCHEAM312.substantiveEvidence: Examines modern and contemporary art from the late nineteenth century to the present together with the institutions that shape its display and reception. Students study avant-gardes, abstraction, modernist design, figuration, postmodern and conceptual practices, and global contemporary art. Museums, exhibitions, curatorial choices and Eurocentric narratives are treated critically. An independently researched paper develops a focused art-historical question, methods and evidence-based argument.
MCCHEAM312.topics: Modernism and avant-gardes; Cubism and abstraction; Modern architecture and design; Figuration and Mexican muralism; Abstract Expressionism; Minimalism and Pop Art; Postmodernism and conceptual art; Photography, installation, performance and video art; Globalization and contemporary art; Authorship, originality and medium; Museums, curating and reception; Eurocentrism in art history
MCCHEAM312.methods: Art-historical interpretation and contextual analysis; Critical analysis of museums and curatorial practices; Scholarly literature review; Independent art-historical research

MCCHEAM315.name: Heritage & Ancient Democracy
MCCHEAM315.substantiveEvidence: Studies Athenian democracy through history, archaeology, literature, art and religion, including its exclusions and moments of crisis. Students analyze citizenship, social divisions, myth, ritual and cultural expression through primary texts and material evidence. A historically grounded assembly simulation explores political decision-making. Research reports connect ancient democracy to the present, while a collective cultural project for Middelburg experiments with participatory democratic collaboration.
MCCHEAM315.topics: Development of Athenian democracy; Citizenship and property classes; Women, foreigners and excluded groups; Democratic reform and participation; Labour and community; Myth, religion and civic identity; Tragedy and satire; Demagoguery, tyranny and democratic resilience; Assembly debate and voting; Ancient and modern democracy; Cultural expression and community
MCCHEAM315.methods: Primary-text and archaeological-evidence analysis; Historical character research; CREATE reading method; Historically grounded assembly simulation; Ancient-modern comparative analysis; Participatory cultural-project design

MCCHEAM316.name: Writing Art's Histories
MCCHEAM316.substantiveEvidence: This course examines the history of art history as an academic discipline, tracing how scholars have understood and interpreted art from the sixteenth century to the present. Through critical readings of influential texts by figures such as Aby Warburg, Erwin Panofsky, Ernst Gombrich, Michel Foucault, and Jacques Derrida, students explore the major ideas and methodologies that have shaped the field. Topics include art and history, aesthetics, meaning and interpretation, authorship and identity, and the challenges of art history in a globalized world.

MCCLITR111.name: Introduction to Literary Studies
MCCLITR111.substantiveEvidence: Introduces practical criticism and literary interpretation through fiction, poetry, drama and contemporary nonfiction, with an introductory component on film adaptation. Students investigate literary value and the constructed character of texts, using concepts of plot, character, setting, point of view, symbolism, style and form. Close reading and engagement with critical sources support analytical presentations and an essay or extended book review.
MCCLITR111.topics: Definitions and value of literature; Literary genre and originality; Story, plot and narrative structure; Character, setting and point of view; Symbolism and allegory; Style, tone, humour and irony; Graphic fiction and microfiction; Creative nonfiction and memoir; Children's literature; Poetic language, imagery, sound and form; Drama and tragedy; Film adaptation
MCCLITR111.methods: Close reading; Formalist literary analysis; Narrative analysis; Poetic and dramatic analysis; Critical-source integration; Literary essay and review construction

MCCLITR112.name: Great Literary Works
MCCLITR112.substantiveEvidence: Surveys major literary works from ancient epic to modern and later fiction, connecting literary form to questions of humanity, mortality, gender, freedom, community and civilization. Students compare genres and recurring motifs through works including Gilgamesh, Greek tragedy, confessional writing, framed tales, philosophical satire, colonial narratives and modernist fiction. Text-focused analysis and engagement with criticism develop interpretation of theme, technique and cultural context.
MCCLITR112.topics: Literature, canon and world literature; Epic and heroism; Tragedy, fate and identity; Autobiography and memory; Framed storytelling and narrative power; Gender and agency; Essay and philosophical tale; Satire and irony; Colonialism and its critique; Modernist narration and subjectivity; Alienation and family; Art, sexuality and civilization; Magical realism
MCCLITR112.methods: Close literary reading; Formalist analysis of genre, theme and technique; Comparative textual interpretation; Narrative analysis; Critical-source interpretation and integration

MCCLITR211.name: World Myth & Literature
MCCLITR211.substantiveEvidence: Compares mythic narratives across ancient and later literary traditions, examining transmission, cultural connections and themes of creation, power, gender, love and loyalty. Greek, Roman, Near Eastern, Indian, Arabic and African materials support comparisons of narrative patterns and representations. Students apply theories of myth and literary analysis in a research paper and graphic explanation, then creatively retell an Ovidian story using another cultural narrative model.
MCCLITR211.topics: Creation and divine succession myths; Myth and cultural power; Gender and exchange; Epic and tragedy; Women, war and narrative agency; Focalization; Hero structures and motifemes; Cross-cultural storytelling; Myth in text, image and performance; Reception and adaptation; Ovid's Metamorphoses
MCCLITR211.methods: Comparative myth analysis; Structuralist narrative analysis and Propp's motifemes; Focalization analysis; Gender-focused literary analysis; Primary-source and scholarly-literature research; Cross-cultural narrative adaptation

MCCLITR212.name: Life & Travel Writing
MCCLITR212.substantiveEvidence: Studies life narrative in literature and popular culture, including memoir, autobiography, diary, personal essay, travel writing and digital self-presentation. Memory, experience, identity, embodiment and agency frame debates about autobiographical truth, fiction, ethics, trauma and cultural positioning. Close readings connect popular, intellectual and migrant memoirs to theory. Students apply analytical concepts in a personal writing portfolio and an independent comparative or focused life-narrative project.
MCCLITR212.topics: Autobiography and memoir culture; Fact, fiction and autobiographical truth; Autobiographical pact; Self and multiple identities; Individual and collective memory; Experience, embodiment and agency; Ethics and traumatic memory; Grief and disability narratives; Popular memoir and narrative technique; Digital self-presentation; Travel and spiritual self-fashioning; Migration, language and cultural identity
MCCLITR212.methods: Close life-narrative analysis; Smith and Watson's strategies for reading life narratives; Theory-guided analysis of memory, identity, embodiment and agency; Comparative textual and contextual interpretation; Structured autobiographical creative writing

MCCLITR311.name: Film & Text
MCCLITR311.substantiveEvidence: Studies the translation of literary narratives into film through formal analysis and adaptation theory. Students compare plot, structure, characterization and setting with cinematic image, acting, editing, music and sound. Medium specificity, fidelity, intertextuality, auteurism, heritage and adaptation markets frame theoretical debates. A substantial research project applies selected concepts to literary and film material, developing an independent interpretation and leading a text- and film-based discussion.
MCCLITR311.topics: Literature-film relationships; Narrative and medium specificity; Fidelity debates; Cinematography and mise-en-scène; Editing, continuity and montage; Film music and sound; Intertextuality; Auteurism; Adaptation and heritage; Adaptation markets; Spectatorship and immersion
MCCLITR311.methods: Formalist literary analysis; Close film-sequence analysis; Comparative text-film analysis; Intertextual analysis; Theory-led adaptation research

MCCLITR312.name: Perspectives on Literary Meaning
MCCLITR312.substantiveEvidence: Examines how different perspectives—humanist, feminist, Marxist, cultural minority and psychoanalytic—affect reading and interpretation. Students undertake a research project applying selected perspectives to texts.

MCCMEDI111.name: Introduction to Film & Media
MCCMEDI111.substantiveEvidence: Introduces how moving images create meaning through cinematography, editing, sound, mise-en-scène, narrative and performance. Film history connects early cinema, Expressionism, montage, Hollywood and New Waves to feminist and postcolonial interpretation. Broader media topics include television, digital platforms, representation and spectatorship. An independent analytical or creative-analytical project combines close analysis, theory, scholarly research and, where chosen, original media work.
MCCMEDI111.topics: Film form and meaning; Cinematography, editing and sound; Mise-en-scène, narrative and performance; Early cinema; German Expressionism and Soviet montage; Classical Hollywood and European New Waves; Feminist film theory; Postcolonial media; Blockbusters; Television and digital platforms; Representation and spectatorship; Media convergence
MCCMEDI111.methods: Close film and media analysis; Historical and cultural contextualization; Application of feminist and postcolonial film theory; Independent analytical or creative-analytical media research

MCCMEDI112.name: Media Archaeology
MCCMEDI112.substantiveEvidence: Examines media technologies as material and cultural artifacts, moving from early print through optical projection, telegraphy, typewriters and analogue sound to digital networks. Students apply recurring theoretical perspectives to how physical properties and infrastructures shape communication, knowledge and memory. Hands-on object, listening and recording exercises connect historical evidence to lived experience. Independent research analyzes a selected media object or phenomenon using appropriate media-archaeological methods.
MCCMEDI112.topics: Media materiality and memory; Print culture; Optics and projection; Telegraphy and infrastructure; Mechanical inscription; Broadcasting and sound fidelity; Portable analogue media; Cassette revival; Computing and networks; Media geology; Technological obsolescence; Mechanical reproduction and aura
MCCMEDI112.methods: Media-archaeological artifact analysis; Historical and technical media comparison; Facsimile and manuscript-print analysis; Media-protocol investigation; Comparative listening and sound-fidelity analysis; Analogue recording exercises; Historical media-object research

MCCMEDI211.name: From T.V. to TikTok
MCCMEDI211.substantiveEvidence: Examines American social history and everyday life from the mid-twentieth century through contemporary media. Storytelling, power and representation connect television, film and digital forms to conformity, identity and imagined futures. Students analyze 1950s media, compare dominant portrayals with Indigenous self-representation, and investigate disability representation. Futures-oriented projects create a speculative television-episode proposal and imagine possibilities that center disabled people.
MCCMEDI211.topics: Media storytelling and power; American everyday life; 1950s television and conformity; Science fiction and social anxieties; Media futures and marginalization; Indigenous representation and self-representation; Disability stereotypes and visibility; Authentic voice and cultural agency; Future foresight and inclusive scenarios
MCCMEDI211.methods: Historical analysis of primary media sources; Comparative representation analysis; Future-foresight scenario development; Theory-based speculative narrative design; Disability-centered futures inquiry

MCCMEDI212.name: Media & the Environment
MCCMEDI212.substantiveEvidence: Examines how visual, audiovisual, sound and digital media shape understanding of ecological problems and human-nonhuman relations. Environmental-humanities concepts guide close analysis of images, narratives and aesthetic strategies across cultural and historical contexts. Students investigate how scientific knowledge, risk and lived experience become representations that influence ethics, public debate and sustainability. A final analytical paper or media-based project develops an argument grounded in course theory.
MCCMEDI212.topics: Environmental representation; Anthropocene; Animal representation and human-nonhuman relations; Deep time and ecological temporality; Biocentrism and environmental justice; Contested ideas of nature; Indigenous and postcolonial media; Ecological risk and scientific knowledge; Environmental affect and perception; Agency, scale and responsibility; Sustainability discourse
MCCMEDI212.methods: Close film, image and sound analysis; Comparative analysis of media forms and representational strategies; Ecocritical interpretation; Theory-based analytical or creative media inquiry

MCCMEDI311.name: Media & Race
MCCMEDI311.substantiveEvidence: Examines racial construction and power in American cultural history from the late nineteenth century to the present through media and popular culture. Theatre, photographs, news, film, music, tourism and literature reveal both oppression and resistance. Students investigate exclusion, racialized bodies, youth, marginalized storytelling and imagined futures. Participant observation, archival research, a documentary podcast and a cross-cultural Photo/Voice project connect historical analysis with lived experience and representation.
MCCMEDI311.topics: Racial construction and whiteness; Media, power and representation; Leisure, tourism and racial identity; Crime, punishment and the racialized body; Asian-American exclusion; Japanese-American incarceration; Childhood and youth; Marginalized and Indigenous storytelling; Racial extremism and propaganda; Alienation and community; Food, environment and cultural nourishment; Afrofuturism and Indigenous futurisms
MCCMEDI311.methods: Participant observation; Archival primary-source research; Historical media analysis; Documentary podcast research, scripting and audio production; Photo/Voice photography and audio narrative; Cross-cultural interpretive reflection

MCCMEDI312.name: The Documentary
MCCMEDI312.substantiveEvidence: Studies documentary history, modes and styles alongside practical documentary production. Students analyze nonfiction representation in historical, social, ethical and aesthetic contexts, from early and Soviet filmmaking through direct cinema and contemporary forms. Topics include propaganda, advocacy, ethnography, history, nature, audio and interactive documentary. Production workshops guide a short film through preproduction, filming and postproduction, with reflection on interviewing and representational choices.
MCCMEDI312.topics: Documentary definition, modes and ethics; Early documentary and city symphonies; Soviet filmmaking; European documentary traditions; Direct cinema and cinéma vérité; Audio and public-affairs documentary; Propaganda and advocacy; Historical and ethnographic documentary; Nature documentary; Mockumentary; Interactive and autobiographical documentary; Documentary aesthetics
MCCMEDI312.methods: Critical documentary analysis; Historical and contextual film comparison; Documentary research and interviewing; Script, storyboard and shot-list development; Preproduction planning; Documentary filming and postproduction; Reflective evaluation of production practice

BENLEAD112.name: Leadership Communication
BENLEAD112.substantiveEvidence: Studies leadership communication through leadership theory, persuasion and practical rhetorical work. Students compare contemporary leadership approaches and examine emotional intelligence, gender, culture and ethics. Literary characters, film and speeches provide material for analyzing effective and ineffective leadership. Students interview a real leader, analyze the leader's communication challenge in an advisory report, and develop a public address presenting their own ethical leadership vision.
BENLEAD112.topics: Leadership models and approaches; Transformational, authentic and adaptive leadership; Servant leadership and followership; Emotional intelligence; Leadership ethics; Gender and culture in leadership; Persuasion and organizational communication; Leadership in literature and film; Storytelling and public speaking; Personal leadership vision
BENLEAD112.methods: Leadership-theory application; Literary and film-based leadership analysis; Professional interviewing and note collection; Leadership-discourse analysis; Communication-advisory report development; Rhetorical speechwriting and storytelling

GOSPHIL111.name: Introduction to Western Philosophy
GOSPHIL111.substantiveEvidence: Introduces major philosophical questions through close study of arguments from ancient Greek thought to contemporary philosophy, with a related Buddhist perspective on the self. Students examine knowledge, ethics, God, mind and consciousness, freedom, identity, time and meaning. Historical texts and contemporary debates, including AI consciousness and concepts of race and gender, develop the ability to reconstruct, evaluate and formulate philosophical arguments in focused essays.
GOSPHIL111.topics: Knowledge, opinion and scepticism; Virtue, duty and consequentialist ethics; Moral objectivity; Existence of God; Idealism and causation; Mind-body problem and consciousness; AI and consciousness; Free will and responsibility; Personal identity and non-self; Existentialism; Race and gender; Time; Meaning of life
GOSPHIL111.methods: Close reading of philosophical texts; Conceptual analysis; Philosophical argument reconstruction and evaluation; Argumentative essay development

GOSPHIL212.name: Ethics
GOSPHIL212.substantiveEvidence: Studies moral reasoning through historical and contemporary ethical theories and close philosophical reading. Utilitarianism, consequentialism, Kantian ethics, virtue ethics, contractarianism and feminist ethics lead into Nietzsche's genealogy, Murdoch's account of goodness and Nagel's treatments of value, perspective, death and meaning. Reflection and research essays require interpretation, argument evaluation and an independent position on ethical theory or a practical ethical problem.
GOSPHIL212.topics: Divine command and human nature; Moral relativism and universalism; Utilitarianism and consequentialism; Kantian ethics; Virtue ethics; Social contract and intuitionism; Feminist and care ethics; Nietzschean genealogy and nihilism; Murdoch's sovereignty of good; Moral value and perspective; Death, absurdity and meaning; Ethical theory and practical judgment
GOSPHIL212.methods: Close philosophical text analysis; Reconstruction and critical evaluation of moral arguments; Comparison of ethical theories; Conceptual analysis; Independent philosophical argument development

GOSPHIL311.name: Philosophy of Emotion
GOSPHIL311.substantiveEvidence: Examines what emotions are and how they shape knowledge, decision-making, ethics, social life and politics. Feeling, cognitive and perceptual theories are compared with historical, phenomenological and contemporary accounts. Love, fear, grief, moods and political anger provide focused cases, alongside emotions in art and their changing relation to time. Students analyze texts and emotional vignettes and develop an independent philosophical paper or a project combining argument with creative work.
GOSPHIL311.topics: Feeling, cognitive and perceptual theories of emotion; Ancient Greek and Indian accounts of emotion; Epistemic emotions; Emotion and decision-making; Love; Fear and existential anxiety; Mood and grief; Moral emotions; Gender and emotion; Political love and anger; Racial injustice; Temporality of emotion; Emotion and artistic expression
GOSPHIL311.methods: Close philosophical reading; Conceptual and argumentative analysis; Phenomenological description of emotional experience; Critical comparison of emotion theories

GOSPOLI111.name: Introduction to Political Philosophy
GOSPOLI111.substantiveEvidence: Surveys political thought from classical antiquity to contemporary debates, including European and non-European thinkers. Students examine views of human nature, society, rights and authority in their historical contexts and compare their proposed solutions with current political problems. Close study of original texts, an individual essay and a group project developing a coherent political philosophy connect historical interpretation to normative argument.
GOSPOLI111.topics: Society, rights and political authority; Classical political thought; Sovereignty and political realism; Enlightenment and revolution; Liberalism and conservatism; Feminism; Nationalism; Socialism and communism; Empire, race and decolonization; Welfare state and libertarianism; Neoliberalism; Justice
GOSPOLI111.methods: Political-text interpretation; Historical contextualization of political ideas; Comparative political argument analysis; Assumption identification; Normative political-theory construction

BENGATE102.name: Research Methods & Statistics
BENGATE102.substantiveEvidence: Introduces empirical research design and statistical analysis, followed by a substantial student research project. Students study operationalization, measurement quality, sampling, surveys and experimental and nonexperimental designs, then descriptive statistics, estimation, hypothesis testing and introductory regression. R and R Commander support data display and analysis. Project teams develop instruments and a research plan, collect and analyze data, and report results under explicit research-ethics and privacy requirements.
BENGATE102.topics: Scientific inquiry and hypotheses; Operationalization and measurement; Reliability and validity; Survey construction and sampling; Randomized and quasi-experimental designs; Nonexperimental and qualitative research; Descriptive statistics; Sampling distributions and estimation; Hypothesis testing and confidence intervals; Association and regression; Research ethics and anonymous data collection
BENGATE102.methods: Survey design; Probability and nonprobability sampling; Experimental and nonexperimental research design; R and R Commander data analysis; Descriptive statistics and visualization; Scale-reliability analysis; One- and two-sample mean tests; ANOVA; Chi-square tests; Correlation and regression; Empirical data collection and analysis

ACCPPDE101.name: Personal & Professional Development
ACCPPDE101.substantiveEvidence: Develops academic writing and research-literacy skills alongside personal development and civic engagement. Students locate and evaluate scholarly sources, synthesize literature, formulate research questions and arguments, and construct a research-paper introduction. A community-engaged project with a societal partner connects these skills to collaboration, reflection and practical contribution. Personal development planning addresses learning goals, self-efficacy, and stress and time management; the course also considers responsible academic use of AI.
ACCPPDE101.topics: Scholarly sources and research questions; Argumentation and thesis statements; Literature synthesis; Academic integrity and referencing; Community engagement; Personal learning goals and reflective learning; Collaborative learning; Self-efficacy; Stress and time management; Responsible use of AI
ACCPPDE101.methods: Scholarly literature searching and source evaluation; Literature synthesis; CARS model for research introductions; Reflective development planning; Community project co-design
